title: Learning Credal Ensembles via Distributionally Robust Optimization
claim: Training an ensemble under varied distribution-shift relaxations yields diverse predictions whose bounds form a credal set capturing epistemic uncertainty.
layout: Left-to-right flow, 2 stages; five colored networks feed stacked simplex panels
description: A left-to-right pipeline diagram. An input image stack on the left feeds a tall rounded box labeled 'Distributionally Robust Optimization, Training Weights δ'. Five arrows leave it, labeled δ1 to δ5, each leading to a small neural network icon drawn in a distinct color (blue, green, orange, pink, purple). The networks feed an 'Inference' vertical box. From there, colored softmax bar charts, one per model, lead to a probability simplex triangle. The triangle shows five colored dots, one per model, and is captioned 'Softmax Probs on Probability Simplex in R^3'. A curved arrow labeled 'Taking Upper & Lower Class Bound' points to a second triangle. It holds a hexagonal box credal set around the same dots, captioned 'Box Credal Set on Probability Simplex'. The background is shaded gray on the left, light blue at top right and light green at bottom right. Color coding links each model to its dot.
caption: CreDRO Concept. ①Training: An ensemble is trained using distributionally robust optimization with members weighted differently to simulate varying degrees of train-test distribution shifts (see Section 3.1). ②Inference: Softmax probabilities are converted into class-wise probability intervals, creating a box credal set (see Section 3.2).
abstract: Credal predictors are models that are aware of epistemic uncertainty and produce a convex set of probabilistic predictions. They offer a principled way to quantify predictive epistemic uncertainty (EU) and have been shown to improve model robustness in various settings. However, most state-of-the-art methods mainly define EU as disagreement caused by random training initializations, which mostly reflects sensitivity to optimization randomness rather than uncertainty from deeper sources. To address this, we define EU as disagreement among models trained with varying relaxations of the i.i.d. assumption between training and test data. Based on this idea, we propose CreDRO, which learns an ensemble of plausible models through distributionally robust optimization. As a result, CreDRO captures EU not only from training randomness but also from meaningful disagreement due to potential distribution shifts between training and test data. Empirical results show that CreDRO consistently outperforms existing credal methods on tasks such as out-of-distribution detection across multiple benchmarks and selective classification in medical applications.
